items.stem: Why keep every assumption in a clearly labelled input cell rather than typed inside formulas?

options.text: So the model can be re-run with new assumptions in one place and audited
options.rationale: Correct: separating inputs makes the model updatable and auditable.

options.text: Because Excel cannot calculate with constants in formulas
options.rationale: Excel calculates with constants fine; this is a modelling discipline.

options.text: To make the file open faster
options.rationale: This is not a performance measure.

options.text: Because Scenario Manager only reads named cells
options.rationale: Scenario Manager can use cell references regardless.

items.explanation: Correct: separating inputs makes the model updatable and auditable.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about Excel What-If tools are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Goal Seek finds the input value that produces a target formula result
options.rationale: Correct: Goal Seek solves for one input to reach a target.

options.text: Scenario Manager can store and switch between sets of input values
options.rationale: Correct: Scenario Manager saves named sets of changing cells.

options.text: A data table permanently replaces the model's base case
options.rationale: A data table reports results; it does not overwrite the base case.

options.text: Goal Seek can solve for multiple inputs at once
options.rationale: Goal Seek changes only one cell; Solver handles multiple.

items.explanation: Correct: Goal Seek solves for one input to reach a target.

items.stem: A two-variable data table is best used to show how one output responds to changes in how many inputs?

options.text: Two inputs varied across rows and columns
options.rationale: Correct: a two-variable data table varies two inputs simultaneously.
That is a one-variable data table.
Data tables support at most two input variables.

options.text: None; it only reformats the output
options.rationale: A data table recomputes results across input combinations.
